organism: Hepatitis A virus (HAV), an RNA picornavirus first isolated in 1979. Humans are the only natural host. HAV is relatively stable at low pH and moderate or frozen temperatures, and can survive in the environment for months, but is inactivated by high temperature (185F/85C or higher), formalin, and chlorine.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is about 28 days (range 15-50). Illness typically has an abrupt onset of fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice, usually resolving within 2 months, though 10%-15% of patients have prolonged or relapsing symptoms lasting up to 6 months. Symptomatic illness is strongly age-dependent: about 70% of infections in children under 6 are asymptomatic, while more than 70% of infections in older children and adults produce jaundice - meaning young children can be an unrecognized source of infection for their household. Severe outcomes are rare but include fulminant hepatitis, with mortality estimates up to 80% for that specific complication; overall case-fatality is 0.3%-0.6% across all ages but up to 1.8% among adults 50 and older.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the only natural reservoir, with no insect or animal vectors and no documented chronic carrier state (though illness can relapse or be prolonged). Transmission is primarily fecal-oral, via contaminated food or water or direct contact with an infected person; rare bloodborne transmission has occurred via transfusion or organ transplant during the illness prodrome. There is no seasonal pattern, though the prevaccine era saw cyclic nationwide epidemics every 10-15 years. Infected people are most contagious 1-2 weeks before illness onset, when fecal viral concentration peaks; risk drops sharply after symptoms begin.
secularTrendsSummary: Hepatitis A became nationally notifiable in 1966; the largest single-year US case count was 59,606 in 1971. Before 2000, incidence was substantially higher in the western US - 11 mostly western states accounted for 50% of cases with only 22% of the population - and children 2-18 historically had the highest rates. Routine ACIP recommendations expanded progressively: high-risk groups in 1996, western-state children in 1999, all US children starting at 12 months in 2006, homelessness in 2019, and all children/adolescents 2-18 plus all persons with HIV in 2020. Cases fell 95.5% from 1996 to 2011, but the disease re-emerged in 2016-2017 through person-to-person outbreaks concentrated among people reporting drug use or homelessness, shifting the burden toward adults 20 and older; more than 37,000 outbreak-associated cases were reported across 35 states from August 2016 through January 2021.
vaccineDescription: HepA vaccines use cell-culture-adapted virus, formalin-inactivated and adsorbed to aluminum hydroxide adjuvant. Single-antigen vaccines (Havrix, licensed 1995; Vaqta, 1996) come in separate pediatric and adult formulations. A combination HepA-HepB vaccine (Twinrix, licensed 2001, adults only) is also available and contains yeast protein. All are given intramuscularly, contain neomycin and no preservative, and some presentations contain latex rubber.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: All children should receive HepA vaccine at 12-23 months, and any previously unvaccinated child or adolescent 2-18 should get catch-up vaccination. The pediatric formulations of Havrix and Vaqta are a 2-dose series (dose 2 at 6-12 months for Havrix, 6-18 months for Vaqta); the same intervals apply to the adult formulations for adults 19+ with risk factors. Twinrix (18+) is a 3-dose series at 0, 1, and 6 months (minimum 4 weeks between doses 1-2, minimum 5 months between doses 2-3), or an accelerated schedule of 0, 7, and 21-30 days with a 12-month booster. The minimum interval between HepA doses 1 and 2 is 6 months, with no maximum interval - a late second dose does not need to be repeated. Vaccines from different manufacturers are considered interchangeable, though completing the series with the same product is preferred when possible.
vaccineEfficacySummary: Both monovalent vaccines are highly immunogenic: more than 95% of adults and more than 97% of children/adolescents develop protective antibody within a month of a single dose, and nearly 100% seroconvert after 2 doses. Clinical efficacy trials found Havrix 94% effective (2 doses, children in Thailand) and Vaqta 100% effective (1 dose, children in New York), both in high-endemicity settings. Duration of protection isn't precisely known, but antibody has been shown to persist at least 20-25 years in vaccinated cohorts, and modeling suggests detectable antibody may persist 40 years or longer.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication; moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution. Twinrix carries the additional contraindications of the hepatitis B vaccine component.
vaccineSafetySummary: The most frequently reported VAERS events for single-antigen HepA vaccines were fever, injection-site erythema, injection-site swelling, and rash; for Twinrix, fever, headache, injection-site pain, and dizziness. A VAERS review found no concerning pattern of adverse events in pregnant women or infants after HepA vaccination during pregnancy; a Vaccine Safety Datalink study similarly found no elevated risk across a range of pregnancy outcomes, though it did find an association with infants being small for gestational age - investigators believe this was likely due to unmeasured confounding but flagged it as worth further study.
vaccineStorageSummary: HepA vaccines must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Because hepatitis A cannot be distinguished from other viral hepatitis on clinical grounds alone, confirmation requires serologic or molecular evidence: the 2019 CSTE case definition requires HAV-specific IgM antibody or a positive nucleic acid amplification test, alongside compatible clinical illness (jaundice or bilirubin >=3 mg/dL, or ALT >200 IU/L with no more likely diagnosis). See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for case-definition and investigation guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Travelers and Immune Globulin (IG)
supplementalTopics.summary: HepA vaccine is recommended for anyone 6 months or older traveling to or working in a country with high or intermediate HAV endemicity. Healthy travelers 12 months through 40 years should get a single dose as soon as travel is planned and complete the series on the routine schedule; travelers over 40, or with immunocompromise or chronic liver disease, should also get a dose as soon as travel is planned, and if departing in under 2 weeks may also receive immune globulin (IG) in a separate limb. Infants 6-11 months traveling internationally should get 1 dose of HepA vaccine that does NOT count toward the routine 2-dose series - the real series still starts at 12 months. Travelers under 6 months, or for whom vaccine is contraindicated or declined, should receive IG instead, dosed by trip length (0.1 mL/kg for up to 1 month, 0.2 mL/kg for up to 2 months, repeated every 2 months thereafter for longer trips).

supplementalTopics.title: Postexposure Prophylaxis
supplementalTopics.summary: Unvaccinated persons 12 months or older exposed to HAV should receive HepA vaccine as soon as possible, within 2 weeks of exposure; a second dose 6 months later is still recommended for long-term protection but is not required for the postexposure response itself. Immunocompromised people or those with chronic liver disease, if unvaccinated and exposed within the past 14 days, should receive both IG (0.1 mL/kg) and vaccine simultaneously at separate sites. IG alone (0.1 mL/kg) is used for postexposure prophylaxis in children under 12 months and anyone for whom vaccine is contraindicated.

supplementalTopics.title: Other Routinely Vaccinated Risk Groups
supplementalTopics.summary: Beyond routine childhood and travel vaccination, ACIP recommends routine HepA vaccination for: all persons 1 year or older experiencing homelessness; persons with chronic liver disease (hepatitis B or C, cirrhosis, fatty liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, or persistently elevated liver enzymes), who are at increased risk of fulminant disease if infected, though not of infection itself; all persons with HIV 1 year or older, for whom postvaccination serologic testing is recommended given possibly reduced response in the immunosuppressed; and previously unvaccinated household or regular contacts of an international adoptee from a high/intermediate-endemicity country, ideally starting the 2-dose series 2+ weeks before the adoptee's arrival. Notably, HepA vaccination is NOT routinely recommended for health care personnel, child care workers, food handlers, or waste-management workers - none of these occupations has been shown to carry elevated risk.

keyPoints: Formerly called 'infectious hepatitis'; differentiated epidemiologically from hepatitis B in the 1940s
Young children are frequently asymptomatic (about 70% under age 6) and can unknowingly spread infection to household contacts
US routine childhood recommendation expanded from 11 high-rate western states (1999) to all 50 states (2006)
Cases fell 95.5% from 1996 to 2011 after vaccine introduction, then re-emerged 2016-2021 via person-to-person outbreaks tied to drug use and homelessness (over 37,000 outbreak-associated cases)
A travel dose given to an infant 6-11 months does not count toward the routine 2-dose series, which must still start at 12 months
Food handlers, health care personnel, and waste-management workers are NOT considered at elevated occupational risk
